source: Belfield, S. and Brown, C. (2010). Guidebook on Upland Crops in Cambodia: Corn (សៀវភៅណែនាំ ស្តីពីដំណាំតំបន់ខ្ពង់រាបនៅក្នុងប្រទេសកម្ពុជា៖ ដំណាំពោត). ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
Corn does not have as narrow a planting window as some crops, but timing still matters a great deal for a reliable stand and yield. Farmers in Cambodia's main corn-growing provinces generally plant twice a year: an early-wet-season (EWS) crop (roughly March-June) and a wet-season (WS) crop (roughly July-August).

Based on a recommended-planting-time chart for Battambang, Pailin, and Kampong Cham provinces, the general pattern is: an earliest-feasible start in March (Pailin) to mid-April (Battambang/Kampong Cham); an optimal window spanning roughly mid/late-March through May depending on province; and a second, shorter optimal window in the wet season, roughly late July through August. Exact week-by-week boundaries differ slightly by province and are best read from the original chart; farmers should treat the specific weekly cut-offs as approximate guidance rather than a fixed calendar, and should still wait for adequate soil moisture (see the rainfall requirements topic) before planting, even within the recommended window.
